newsitem.title: USA: Despite name, Giant plans for modest growth.
newsitem.headline: Despite name, Giant plans for modest growth.

text.p: Despite its name, oil refiner Giant Industries Inc. of Scottsdale, Ariz., isn't fuelled by grandiose plans for expansion.

These days, as most U.S. refiners merge or expand at a voracious rate, Giant is staying within its territory and traditional strengths, Jim Acridge, the company's founder and chief executive, said in an interview.

"We don't get caught up in what someone else is doing. We try to play to our own strengths and build on what we feel we can do better than someone else. We stay away from things we know we can't compete in," Acridge said.

The 35-year-old company, which runs two small refineries in rural New Mexico, hopes to reach revenues of $1 billion over the next year -- small in an industry where the largest participants see annual sales in the hundreds of billions.

As aggressive refiners like Tosco Corp. and Ultramar Diamond Shamrock Corp. encroach on its territory, the small refiner has decided to take modest steps to expand its presense in its home territory, the ever-more lucrative Southwest.
The company has spent part of its $80 million capital budget this year to raise gasoline production by 25 percent, or 1,500 barrels per day (bpd), at its two refineries.
"It provides additional (gasoline) volume for us to be able to expand our market share as our market grows," Acridge said, adding the facility earlier produced gasoline at a rate of 26,000 bpd.

Production will also increase next year after the company adds equipment to its refinery in Ciniza, N.M., which will convert natural gas liquids into gasoline. The upgrade will add 3,500 barrels per day to the company's gasoline output.
Giant is also shopping throughout the 10-state Rocky Mountain region for another refinery in the 50,000- to 75,000-bpd range.

Increased production will help feed Giant's growing retail chain, which jumped from 52 service stations to 148 after the company spent $16 million to acquire sites from Thriftway Marketing Corp. in April.
Thirteen more gas stations are on slate for construction this year, Acridge said, bringing captial spending to $100 million, compared with net revenues of nearly $500 million in 1996.

Giant, which prides itself on delivering gasoline and other petroleum products to rural markets deprived of pipelines, said it hopes to hire four to five more trucking distributers, or jobbers, to supply its company-owned stores and independent dealers.
"To ... make (independents) want to brand Giant rather than Diamond Shamrock or Phillips we need to have a formal programme and that's what we're in the throes of putting together," Acridge said.
Jobbers allow the company to expand its distribution without heavy outlays of cash.
"As an independent ... we can compete very effectively with the major oil company's jobbers," Acridge said, explaining has the advantage of more local sales staff in the more rural areas it serves.
"I feel like we're on a spring board and there's a lot of opportunity out there," Acridge said.
